items.title: No shared definition of engagement
items.whyItMatters: Twenty-three measures make studies incomparable (claim c2).
items.opportunity: Chart each study's definition and whether it measured features, duration or both.

items.title: Engagement rarely followed beyond three months
items.whyItMatters: Most people stop within weeks (claim c1), so short studies overstate engagement.
items.opportunity: Chart follow-up length for every engagement estimate.

items.title: Clinician response is rarely studied as a feature
items.whyItMatters: People stop when nobody looks at their entries (claim c3), which bears directly on nurse coaching.
items.opportunity: Chart whether and how clinicians responded to app data.

items.title: People without access or with intellectual disability
items.whyItMatters: Smartphone ownership is lower in older and low-income patients (claim c4) and trials excluded people with intellectual disability.
items.opportunity: Chart who was offered an app and who was excluded.

items.title: Outcomes linked to engagement are sparse
items.whyItMatters: No trial showed an effect on seizures.
items.opportunity: Chart outcomes reported with engagement without implying causation.

errorsFound: The clinic's plan assumes coaching raises engagement enough to change outcomes; no retrieved record shows that link.
reevaluation: The gaps favour a scoping review that charts definitions, duration, clinician response, access and the outcomes reported.
summary: Five gaps: definitions, follow-up length, clinician response, equity of access and sparse outcomes.
